topic: AI Tech Mystery: When Cuneiform Met Modern Slang
framing_note: Research supports AI-assisted transliteration, OCR, and Akkadian-to-English translation experiments. It does not show that ancient cuneiform texts contain modern slang or that AI translations are authoritative without expert review. Any modern-slang version must be clearly labelled as a creative adaptation, not a literal translation.

sources.title: Translating Akkadian to English with neural machine translation
sources.review_anchor: Abstract; methods; results; limitations and supplementary material
sources.relevance: Presents neural machine translation for Akkadian from cuneiform Unicode glyphs and transliteration to English. Reports BLEU4 scores of 36.52 and 37.47 for the two tasks and stronger performance on short/medium sentences.
sources.limitations: BLEU is an automatic similarity metric, not a guarantee of a correct translation. The authors describe human-in-the-loop correction and limitations by sentence length.

sources.title: Reading Akkadian cuneiform using natural language processing
sources.relevance: Presents NLP methods for automatic transliteration and segmentation of Unicode cuneiform glyphs; reports accuracy up to 97% for that specific task.
sources.limitations: The reported 97% is for transliteration/segmentation, not end-to-end translation into English or modern slang.

sources.title: CuReD: Deep Learning Optical Character Recognition for Cuneiform Text Editions and Legacy Materials
sources.publication: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Machine Learning for Ancient Languages (ML4AL 2024), pp. 130–140
sources.review_anchor: Abstract; dataset description; evaluation; PDF pp. 130–140
sources.relevance: Describes a human-in-the-loop deep-learning OCR pipeline for digitizing scanned transliterations of cuneiform texts, with character error rates of 9% on clean data and 11% on representative scans.
sources.limitations: The pipeline reads scanned editions/transliterations, not raw clay tablets directly. Character error rate is not translation accuracy.

sources.title: Machine Learning for Ancient Languages: A Survey
sources.review_anchor: Survey taxonomy and sections on digitization, restoration, translation, and decipherment
sources.relevance: Surveys machine-learning tasks in ancient-text scholarship and emphasizes interdisciplinary collaboration between humanities specialists and machine-learning researchers.
sources.limitations: A survey is field context, not direct validation of a particular translation model.

candidate_claims.text: A 2023 study presented neural machine-translation models for Akkadian-to-English translation from cuneiform Unicode glyphs and transliteration.
The 2023 Akkadian translation study reported BLEU4 scores of 36.52 and 37.47 for its two translation tasks and identified stronger performance on short and medium-length sentences.
A 2020 study reported up to 97% accuracy for automatic transliteration and segmentation of standard Unicode cuneiform glyphs into words.
A 2024 project developed a human-in-the-loop OCR pipeline for scanned cuneiform text editions and reported 9% character error on clean data and 11% on representative scans.

unsupported_claims: The AI system can reliably translate every cuneiform tablet without expert review.
The original Akkadian texts contain modern slang.
A 97% transliteration/segmentation accuracy result means 97% translation accuracy.
OCR of scanned transliterations is the same as reading a photograph of an unprocessed clay tablet.
reviewer_instructions: Read each paper's methods, evaluation data, and limitations.
Keep transliteration, segmentation, OCR, and translation as distinct technical tasks.
Do not treat BLEU scores as human translation accuracy.
Use a human-in-the-loop caveat and describe the systems as research tools.
If modern slang is used in narration, label it as a humorous paraphrase/adaptation, never as a literal translation.
No claim enters the evidence ledger until a human reviewer approves the source and records an exact reference.
